For a more comprehensive discussion of these guidelines, as well as information on infections that are not sexually transmitted, refer to the Guidelines for Perinatal Care. 3. The sources for screening guidelines for pregnant women include the Guide to Clinical Preventive Services, Guidelines for Perinatal Care, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) Technical Bulletin on Gonorrhea and Chlamydial Infections, Recommendations for the Prevention and Management of Chlamydia trachomatis Infections, and Hepatitis B Virus: A Comprehensive Strategy for Eliminating Transmission in the United States through Universal Childhood Vaccination by the Immunization Practices Advisory Committee (ACIP). 4. These sources are not entirely consistent in their recommendations. 5. The Guide to Clinical Preventive Services recommends screening high-risk patients for chlamydia but notes that the optimal timing for screening remains uncertain. 6. The Guidelines for Perinatal Care recommend that pregnant women at high risk for chlamydia be screened during their first prenatal visit and again during the third trimester. 7. Recommendations for screening pregnant women for sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) are based on factors such as disease severity, potential complications, prevalence in the population, costs, legal considerations (e.g., state laws), and other factors. 8. The screening recommendations in this report are more extensive than other guidelines, meaning more women would be screened for a broader range of STDs if these recommendations are followed. These recommendations are also compatible with other CDC guidelines. 9. Physicians should choose a screening strategy that aligns with the population and setting of their medical practice and meets their goals for STD case detection and treatment. Adolescents 10. Health-care providers caring for adolescents should be aware of specific issues related to this population. 11. Adolescents have the highest rates of many STDs, such as gonorrhea, which is most prevalent among females aged 15–19 years. 12. Clinic-based studies show that the prevalence of chlamydial infections, and possibly human papillomavirus (HPV) infections, is also highest among adolescents. 13. Surveillance data indicate that 9% of adolescents with acute hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection either had sexual contact with a chronically infected person or multiple sex partners or identified as homosexual. 14. As part of a comprehensive strategy to eliminate HBV transmission in the United States, ACIP recommends that all children receive the hepatitis B vaccine. 15. Adolescents at high risk for STDs include male homosexuals, sexually active heterosexuals, clients in STD clinics, and injecting drug users. 16. Younger adolescents (e.g., those under 15 years old) who are sexually active are at particular risk for infection. 17. Adolescents are at the greatest risk for STDs due to frequent unprotected intercourse, biological susceptibility to infection, and barriers to accessing health care. 18. Clinicians providing services to adolescents can address these issues by improving knowledge and awareness about STD risks and consequences, offering guidance to promote healthy sexual behaviors, and preventing the establishment of harmful patterns of behavior. 19. In the United States, with limited exceptions, adolescents can consent to confidential STD diagnosis and treatment without parental consent or knowledge. 20. In many states, adolescents can also consent to HIV counseling and testing. 21. Consent laws for adolescent vaccination vary by state, with some states allowing vaccination services without parental consent, treating it similarly to STD treatment. 22. 23. Counseling and health education for adolescents should be tailored to their developmental level and address risky behaviors, such as sexual activity and drug use. 24. Careful, nonjudgmental counseling and thorough discussions are particularly important for adolescents who may not acknowledge engaging in high-risk behaviors. Children 25. Managing children with STDs requires close collaboration between clinicians, laboratory personnel, and child-protection authorities. 26. Investigations, when indicated, should be initiated promptly. 27. Certain diseases, such as gonorrhea, syphilis, and chlamydia, if acquired after the neonatal period, are almost always indicative of sexual contact. 28. For other diseases, such as HPV infection and vaginitis, the association with sexual contact is less clear. HIV Infection: Detection, Initial Management, and Referral 29. HIV infection progresses through a spectrum of disease, from a clinically latent or asymptomatic state to AIDS as the late manifestation. 30. The rate of disease progression varies, with the time from HIV infection to AIDS development ranging from a few months to as long as 17 years (median: 10 years). 31. Most adults and adolescents with HIV remain symptom-free for long periods, but viral replication is active throughout all stages of infection and increases significantly as the immune system deteriorates. 32. AIDS eventually develops in nearly all HIV-infected individuals. In one study, 87% of HIV-infected adults developed AIDS within 17 years of infection. 33. Additional cases are expected among those who have remained AIDS-free for longer periods. 34. Increased awareness of HIV transmission risk factors among patients and health-care providers has led to more frequent HIV testing and earlier diagnosis, often before symptoms develop. 35. Early diagnosis of HIV infection is crucial for several reasons: Treatments are available to slow the decline of immune system function. HIV-infected individuals with altered immune function are at increased risk for preventable infections, such as Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia, toxoplasmic encephalitis, disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex disease, tuberculosis, and bacterial pneumonia. HIV affects the diagnosis, evaluation, treatment, and follow-up of many other diseases and may influence the efficacy of antimicrobial therapy for some STDs. 36. Early diagnosis also allows health-care providers to counsel patients and assist in preventing HIV transmission to others. 37. Proper management of HIV infection involves a complex array of behavioral, psychosocial, and medical services. 38. While some of these services may be available in STD treatment facilities, others, particularly medical services, are often unavailable in such settings. 39. Referral to a health-care provider or facility experienced in managing HIV-infected patients is recommended. 40. Staff in STD treatment facilities should be knowledgeable about referral options available in their communities.
